one-check-per-line.why: all 6 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 6

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 6 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: Check 3 breaks the criterion. Its expect line gives exit 1 for a bad row and exit 2 for an unreadable file, but doesn't say which wins when both happen. Check 3's PASS still requires exit=2 for "c1 missing b1" in both commands, ranking a read error above bad rows. The brief's own Advisory lists "A read error should win over bad rows for the exit code (2)", so it treats the rule as advisory yet grades on it. Check 4 is also arguably too strict: its PASS needs one exact lint output string whose error text depends on the Node version, which "unchanged" doesn't require. Check 5 is borderline: it requires the README to document the exit codes, but the expect line only says "documents the usage". Checks 1, 2 and 6 stay within their expect lines.

runs-as-written.why: The criterion holds for both briefs. Every path they use is tracked at this commit or created earlier in the same command: bin/jsonl-lint.js, src/index.js, test/cli.test.js, the README and .github/workflows/test.yml. The verifier's checks make their temp files with mktemp before reading them. The shell syntax is valid: the &&/; chains and printf are fine, the escaped quotes in `node -e "import('./packages/...')..."` come out as valid JavaScript, and the jq filters (`(.body // "")`, `\(.name)`) are well formed. `git rev-parse HEAD:path` and `npm test --workspace packages/jsonl-lint` are valid commands. The grep -e patterns are valid regex, and the gh api endpoints exist. One weak spot: the builder's hand test `... a.jsonl - b.jsonl` names files that don't exist. It still runs (it would just report a read error), and it says "with real files", so the builder is meant to supply them. That doesn't break the criterion.

catches-traps.why:
I checked all four must_catch items and each one is handled.
1. Check 3's second command runs `c1.jsonl missing.jsonl b1.jsonl` in one call. It requires "exit=2, stdout containing `<d>/b1.jsonl:1: ...`" and the error naming missing.jsonl on stderr, so the combined case is tested, not only each case alone.
2. Check 4 runs `git rev-parse HEAD:packages/jsonl-lint/src/index.js` at the head and compares the result with the base file's blob hash (83cbf9f…). If the hash differs, the verifier must look at the diff to src/index.js. This compares the head with the base, not just the file's current text.
3. Builder step 5 says "Update packages/jsonl-lint/README.md" and lists the usage, `-` for stdin and the exit codes.
4. Check 6 uses the GitHub API to find the PR whose body contains the Closes URL and confirms its head sha matches the commit checked. It also requires the `test` check run at that sha to be "completed success".

avoids-must-not.why: Checked each verifier PASS/FAIL condition against must_not. Checks 1–3 run the CLI on temporary files and stdin and compare output and exit codes. Nothing passes on reading the code ("reading the diff alone is not enough"). No condition needs exact stderr wording: check 2 needs only "a message on stderr (not a lint line)" with exit=2. Check 3's "error naming missing.jsonl" is a reasonable reading of "error on stderr", not exact wording. No branch-name rule, mutation test or file-touch limit appears. Check 4's blob hash has a fallback: a different hash still passes if lint's text is identical. The builder's "that literal text" for the README is an instruction to the builder. Verifier check 5 only needs the README to document the usage, so it is not a stricter pass condition. Advisory items are marked not pass/fail.

methods-private.why: The builder brief carries the verifier's checks. Step 5 tells the builder the README Usage must show "`<file> [<file> ...]` (that literal text)" and to write "`-` reads stdin" in backticks. Those are exactly the two patterns the verifier's check 5 greps for ('<file> \[<file> \.\.\.\]' and '`-`'), so the builder is shaped around the grep probe. Step 4 also repeats verifier PASS conditions as test requirements. "a bad file after the missing one still reported on stdout" and "message on stderr naming it" match check 3's second command. "two bad files checking their lines appear in argument order" matches check 1's ordering condition. "a read error wins over bad rows" matches check 3's expected exit=2 for c1/missing/b1. The hand-run command in step 6 is a different input from the verifier's, and telling the builder to run npm test is allowed. Even so, the leaked grep literal and the copied pass conditions break the criterion.
